name: Oxygen partial pressure
explanation: The pressure of oxygen alone: total cabin pressure times the oxygen fraction. Low-pressure habitats raise the O₂ percentage to keep enough oxygen to breathe, which is the trade-off between crew health and fire risk.
steps: Take the cabin pressure P from the preset or the pressure slider, in kPa.
Turn the oxygen percentage into a fraction: x(O₂) = O₂ % ÷ 100.
Multiply: pO₂ = P × x(O₂). We show it next to ISS air (101.3 kPa × 0.21) for comparison.

example.text: NASA's proposed exploration atmosphere for Moon and Mars habitats (8.2 psia, 34 % O₂)

limits: A definition, valid for any mix. It does not say how fast a fire spreads: at the same pO₂, a higher O₂ percentage at lower total pressure can still burn more readily.

sources.title: Effects of the 8 psia / 32% O2 Atmosphere on the Human in the Spaceflight Environment
sources.locator: PDF p. 11 (inspired O₂ partial pressure of the 8.2/34 and 10.2/26.5 atmospheres)

name: Droplet d² law
expression: d² = d₀² − K · t   →   t_burn = d₀² ÷ K
explanation: A burning droplet's diameter squared falls in a straight line with time. FLEX measured the slope K (the burning-rate constant) for each test, so the time a droplet lasts follows from its starting size.

variables.meaning: time for the droplet to burn away (d = 0)

whereUsed.label: Flame Lab › Nearest NASA tests › “A 2 mm droplet lasts”

steps: Find the FLEX tests closest to your setting: same fuel, O₂ within ±2 points, pressure within ±20 %.
Take the median of their measured burning-rate constants K (needs at least 3 tests).
Set d = 0 in the d² law and solve for time: t_burn = d₀² ÷ K, with d₀ = 2 mm.
Only shown in microgravity and inside the FLEX range; otherwise the lab says the conditions were never tested.

example.text: A 2 mm droplet with K = 0.6 mm²/s (a typical FLEX value in ISS-like air)

limits: Assumes the droplet burns to the end. Many FLEX flames went out first (extinction), so the real flame time can be shorter. Not tested under gravity, below 70 kPa or above 34 % O₂.

sources.title: Detailed Results From the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) March 2009 to December 2011 (NASA/TP—2015-216046)
sources.locator: p. 19, column definitions: burning rate from a linear fit of droplet diameter squared versus time; K per test in Table IX, pp. 20–28

name: Forced stretch rate (flame blowoff)
explanation: How hard the oncoming airflow strains the flame at the tip of a burning rod. Too much stretch and the flame blows off; NASA used it to compare blowoff in normal gravity with BASS-II results from the ISS.

variables.meaning: average flow speed entering the tube

steps: Take the airflow speed U that reaches the flame and the radius r of the burning rod.
Compute a = 1.5 × U ÷ r. A larger a means the flow pulls harder on the flame.
In NASA's tests, the stretch rate at blowoff varied linearly with oxygen and as the square root of the rod radius (p. 3).
Explained only for now: the site doesn't compute it, because the Flame Lab's fuels are droplets, not PMMA rods.

example.text: A 0.635 cm radius PMMA rod in a 20 cm/s flow

limits: Measured in normal gravity on cast PMMA rods, 15–18 % O₂, flows up to 60.3 cm/s. The paper's 14 % O₂ data were discarded. Not a general flammability limit for other materials.

sources.title: Correlation of normal gravity mixed convection blowoff limits with microgravity forced flow blowoff limits (Marcum, Olson, Ferkul, 2016)
sources.locator: p. 3 (stretch rate definition); p. 1 abstract and p. 2 (rod sizes, O₂ range, 60.3 cm/s maximum flow)
